title: Financial Incisors: Cutting Through the Effects of Private Equity on Dentistry Market Dynamics and Care Delivery
pub: Health Services Research 61(2):1–12 (April 2026 issue; online first 10 December 2025)
author: Kamyar Nasseh · Anthony T. LoSasso · Marko Vujicic · Tim Downey

dom.t: Healthcare ownership: Financial gains do not prove patient benefit

st.t: Healthcare ownership: Financial gains do not prove patient benefit
st.an: The dentistry study directly supports the cluster’s proposition by distinguishing increased list charges and revenue-oriented service shifts from negotiated prices and demonstrated patient or provider benefits. It treats welfare gains as unproven rather than inferring them from improved practice finances.
qs: **Principle Findings.** Following acquisition, private equity-owned dental offices increased charges for dental care services by 3.3% (95% CI: 2.3%–4.4%), although allowed prices for these services remained statistically unchanged.
In other words, financial enhancement of dental practices under private equity may not translate into benefits for providers or patients.

kp.k: Practice-level acquisition study uses staggered difference-in-differences
kp.d: The authors examine private equity ownership in dentistry using a proprietary dental office database linked to administrative commercial claims and a staggered difference-in-differences panel design intended to address nonrandom acquisitions. Sources comprise private equity transactions from 2015 to 2021, American Dental Association dental office data from 2015 to 2017 and 2019 to 2021, and aggregated commercial insurance price and utilization data from 2015 to 2021. These are findings about dentistry, not direct evidence about AI or legal services.
qs: We utilize a proprietary dental office database linked to administrative dental commercial claims data to estimate the effects of private equity ownership on the financial and operational outcomes of dental offices, employing a staggered difference-in-differences panel design that addresses the nonrandom acquisitions of facilities by private equity firms.

We rely on private equity transaction data from 2015 to 2021, longitudinal dental office data from the 2015 to 2017 and 2019 to 2021 American Dental Association dental office database, and aggregated commercial dental insurance price and utilization data from 2015 to 2021.

kp.k: Charges rose, but negotiated prices remained statistically unchanged
kp.d: Following acquisition, private equity-owned dental offices increased charges by 3.3% (95% CI: 2.3%–4.4%), while allowed prices remained statistically unchanged. The authors distinguish list prices from prices negotiated between dentists and payers, arguing that higher list prices can still be passed on to patients; the abstract does not quantify actual patient payments.
qs: Following acquisition, private equity-owned dental offices increased charges for dental care services by 3.3% (95% CI: 2.3%–4.4%), although allowed prices for these services remained statistically unchanged.
Allowed or negotiated prices between dentists and payers did not change in dental offices after being acquired by private equity.
Nevertheless, list prices for dental services increased in private equity-owned practices, meaning higher prices can still be passed on to patients.

kp.k: Service mix shifted toward higher-reimbursement procedures
kp.d: Acquired offices tended to move away from diagnostic and preventive procedures toward generally higher-reimbursement restorative, specialty, and surgical procedures. The authors identify this service-mix shift as a mechanism through which private equity can enhance practice revenue without higher provider reimbursement. The abstract supplies no numerical estimate of the shift.
qs: Dental offices acquired by private equity firms tended to shift from diagnostic and preventive procedures to generally higher reimbursement restorative, specialty, and surgical procedures.
Private equity firms can enhance dental practice revenue by shifting from preventive procedures to higher-cost restorative procedures while not reimbursing providers at a higher amount.

kp.k: Acquisition increased likelihood of multispecialty practice
kp.d: The study reports that dental offices were more likely to become multispecialty practices after private equity acquisition, indicating an organizational change alongside the reported change in procedure mix. The abstract does not report the magnitude of this effect.
qs: Dental offices were more likely to become multispecialty practices after being acquired by a private equity firm.

kp.k: Financial gains may not benefit providers or patients
kp.d: The authors caution that financial enhancement under private equity may not translate into benefits for providers or patients and recommend policymaker attention to acquisition effects on their welfare. This is a qualified interpretation and policy recommendation, rather than a quantified finding of patient or provider harm.
qs: In other words, financial enhancement of dental practices under private equity may not translate into benefits for providers or patients.
Policymakers should be aware of the effects private equity acquisition has on provider and patient welfare.

kp.k: Abstract-only evidence leaves Medicaid participation findings unavailable
kp.d: Although Medicaid participation is a stated study objective, the supplied abstract reports no result for that outcome. The held document contains only the structured abstract, with the paywalled article body unavailable, limiting extraction to the methods, findings, and conclusions reported there.
qs: To assess how private equity ownership affects prices, service mix, and Medicaid participation in dentistry at the practice level.
The structured abstract above is the whole of the held text; the article body is paywalled and not on file.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Nasseh, LoSasso, Vujicic and Downey report that private equity acquisition changes dental practices’ charges, service mix and specialty structure, without a statistically significant change in allowed prices.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain source about private equity in dentistry, not AI or legal services. The authors report a 3.3% increase in charges following acquisition, a shift away from diagnostic and preventive procedures toward generally higher-reimbursement restorative, specialty and surgical procedures, and an increased likelihood of becoming a multispecialty practice. They distinguish list charges from allowed or negotiated prices, which remained statistically unchanged. They further argue that higher list prices can be passed on to patients and that revenue enhancement through service-mix changes may not benefit providers or patients; these are qualified implications rather than separately quantified welfare findings in the available abstract.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The authors base their findings on linked practice, transaction and commercial insurance data analyzed using a staggered difference-in-differences panel design.
pts.d: The abstract describes a proprietary dental office database linked to administrative commercial dental claims, together with private equity transaction data. The authors state that their design addresses nonrandom acquisition of facilities. The charge increase is accompanied by a 95% confidence interval; the abstract reports statistical non-change for allowed prices but provides no effect sizes or confidence intervals for service-mix or multispecialty outcomes. Only the structured abstract is available, so further methodological details and results cannot be extracted.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The claims concern post-acquisition outcomes within historical data covering 2015–2021, not a forecast of future market changes.
pts.d: Transaction and commercial insurance data cover 2015–2021; dental office observations cover 2015–2017 and 2019–2021. The abstract does not specify the duration of post-acquisition effects or their persistence beyond the observation period. Findings are conditional on private equity acquisition and the measured dental-office outcomes. 'Statistically unchanged' allowed prices should not be read as proof of exactly zero price effect. Potential patient price exposure and lack of welfare benefits are expressed using 'can' and 'may,' rather than as universal outcomes.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The authors identify acquired dental practices, private equity owners, dental providers, payers and patients as affected, and flag implications for policymakers.
pts.d: Acquired practices change their charges, procedure mix and specialty organization. Private equity owners can enhance practice revenue through a shift toward higher-cost procedures. Payers’ negotiated or allowed prices remain statistically unchanged in the reported findings, while patients may face higher list prices. The authors caution that practice-level financial gains may not translate into provider or patient benefits and call for policymaker attention to welfare effects. Medicaid participation is listed as a study objective, but the held abstract supplies no finding about it. No specific patient subgroup or measured care-quality effect is reported.
